section_1.title: The Hook: Why Models Matter
section_1.content: Introduce the concept of infectious disease dynamics. Define the objective: using mathematics to predict how quickly a virus spreads through a population.
section_1.example: Imagine a flu outbreak in a school of 100 students. How do we predict if 10 or 90 will get sick?

section_2.title: Defining the Components: The S-I-R Framework
section_2.content: Break down the population into three compartments: Susceptible (S), Infectious (I), and Recovered/Removed (R). Emphasize that these states are mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive.
section_2.example: Visualize a colored marble analogy: Blue (S), Red (I), and Green (R). An I-marble 'bumps' into an S-marble, turning it Red.

section_3.title: The Engine of Change: Differential Equations
section_3.content: Explain the transition rates: S to I (infection rate) and I to R (recovery rate). Introduce the visual flow: S -> I -> R, noting that I drives the flux of S into R.
section_3.example: Graph visualization showing an S-curve declining, an I-curve spiking (the 'hump'), and an R-curve climbing steadily.

section_4.title: The Threshold of Chaos: Understanding R0
section_4.content: Explain the Basic Reproduction Number (R0). If R0 > 1, the epidemic grows; if R0 < 1, it dies out. Connect this to the balance of infection and recovery rates.
section_4.example: Compare two scenarios: a 'highly contagious' virus (one person infects 5) vs. a 'slower' virus (one person infects 0.8).

section_5.title: Summary and Real-World Application
section_5.content: Synthesize how the SIR model allows us to simulate interventions like social distancing or vaccination. Final takeaway: Models are lenses that help us make informed decisions.
section_5.example: Show a simulation where 'social distancing' reduces the peak of the I-curve, preventing the healthcare system from being overwhelmed.
